cim: Inside the algorithms: How artificial intelligence is enhancing traditional pathology practice

cim_eredeti: Inside the algorithms: How artificial intelligence is enhancing traditional pathology practice
szoveg_eredeti:
When a patient needs a second opinion, how does the biopsied tissue travel? The answer is surprisingly analog for 2026. Glass slides containing biological materials are often carried between offices so multiple pathologists can take a look.

According to Lee Cooper, director of computational pathology at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, digital imaging methods are becoming more popular in the field of pathology. After a sample of blood or tissue is taken from a patient and placed on a glass slide, the slide is inserted into a scanner that produces a digital image that can be shared electronically.

In addition to enabling frictionless travel, digitized samples can be reviewed by artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms. Cooper, who runs a lab in which researchers develop such algorithms, says the algorithms will help pathologists make more accurate and detailed diagnoses, as well as help researchers interpret how diseases have progressed in past patients.

“We develop tools to interpret these images,” Cooper said. “It could be for scientific purposes, like somebody wants to study inflammation, or it could be for a clinical purpose, like someone wants to make sure that a diagnosis is correct.”

The appeal of digital pathology, according to Cooper, is a computer can analyze a sample in much greater detail than a human can. “In each image there could be a million cells, or more than a million cells,” he said. “Precisely measuring that is very hard for humans to do.”

Researchers in the Cooper Lab spend their time writing algorithms, digitizing specimens and analyzing the resulting images. They review samples obtained through ongoing research studies as well as previously banked samples to look backward and better understand how diseases progress in patients.

Each researcher focuses on developing algorithms for a unique data set or to address a specific problem that pathologists face.

Researcher Fattaneh Pourakpour’s digitized tissue data comes from Northwestern’s Mesulam Institute for Cognitive Neurology and Alzheimer’s Disease brain bank, which accepts brain donations upon death from people who had dementia.

Pourakpour, a Ph.D. student in electrical engineering at Northwestern, develops two main types of artificial intelligence algorithms. Her tissue segmentation algorithms distinguish the different regions of the brain, such as gray matter and white matter, from each other. Meanwhile, her cell classifier algorithms identify different cell types within the gray matter and then categorize them.

Pourakpour also works on feature engineering, which is a way of using raw data to create predictive models. “We are trying to find new insights into neurodegenerative disorders by analyzing this pathology data,” Pourakpour said. “And to see if there are any special biomarkers associated with Alzheimer’s disease and neurodegenerative disorders.”

Another researcher, Ramin Nateghi, applies machine learning to prostate cancer detection.

“AI has the potential to discover subtle changes in cancer that aren’t visible to the human eye,” said Nateghi, a post-doctoral researcher who holds a Ph.D. in electrical engineering from Shiraz University of Technology in Shiraz, Iran. Prostate cancer often progresses slowly, requiring careful analysis. “If you look at biopsies taken over time, you might not see many differences in over 25 years,” he said. “So, what is important here for us is to use these tools and try to detect subtle changes in the slides. It can help doctors make better decisions.”

Digital pathology tools are not meant to replace pathologists but instead augment their work. “There are reasons why you can’t really replace human pathologists,” Cooper said.

One reason is the existence of difficult edge cases. “The type of data and models that I work with operate on the basis of correlation,” Cooper said. “There is no causal understanding inside of these models.” This means that an algorithm’s utility is limited by the data it is trained on. Therefore, an algorithm will be less helpful when it reviews a rare case that it has never seen before.

Whether models possess deep understandings of the subjects they are trained in, or simply understand them at superficial levels, is an unanswered question. Cooper said he thinks they can be useful for delivering accurate and efficient predictions regardless. Computers can consider many more properties of the samples than a doctor could, which can help it generate a fuller prediction of that patient’s future. However, “I don’t think they should be trusted implicitly,” Cooper said.

Pathology data is by far the biggest source of data in the medical field. According to Cooper, the Northwestern Medicine health care system generates about 2 million glass slides per year.

“We have a huge shortage of pathologists (in the United States), but heaps and heaps of patient biopsy data that needs to be inspected, analyzed, reviewed by pathologists to then determine what further testing needs to be done,” said researcher Lawrence Chillrud, a Ph.D. student in electrical engineering at Northwestern.

Chillrud develops tools geared toward maximizing the efficiency and accuracy of a pathologist’s practice. His models conduct a preliminary screen of pathology data to sort out the most obvious cases while flagging others for fast-tracked, specialized review.

Similar algorithms might sort out the hardest cases and balance them across a group of pathologists or put them early in a pathologist’s workflow. They might also count the occurrence of different items within the sample, such as a certain kind of cell; direct the pathologist’s attention to important areas of the sample; or review a pathologist’s report for potential errors.

Chillrud is also developing uncertainty tools, which quantify the likely accuracy of a model’s prediction. “A lot of these models are overconfident, and they’ll give a kind of false picture of how well you can trust their predictions,” Chillrud said. An uncertainty tool would flag for the pathologist any results with a high probability of error, giving pathologists insight into when they should ignore a model’s predictions.

Uncertainty tools can also help reduce bias in artificial intelligence.

A common phrase in artificial intelligence development is “garbage in, garbage out.” This means if a model is trained on a data set that includes a sampling bias, selection bias or other flaw, the model will inherit those same issues.

“A lot of these models will inherit the biases of the data sets they’re trained on,” Chillrud said. “If you’re training on mostly white, affluent patients living in a certain part of the city, because those are the patients that tend to come into your hospital, then your model won’t be as good at making predictions about patients from different backgrounds.” With uncertainty tools, a model can alert a pathologist when its predictions might be impacted by gaps in its knowledge.

Artificial intelligence pathology tools can also help address shortages of specialized pathologists. A general pathologist might not have the training to give a detailed read of a prostate cancer biopsy, for example. While large, city-based medical systems might have specialized pathologists on staff, specialists are harder to find in smaller, more rural areas.

Despite the promises of digital pathology, Cooper isn’t sure how quickly it will become commonplace. For one, digital pathology tools must undergo FDA clearance, and be validated on very high-quality data, which can be hard to access. Secondly, not all medical systems have adopted the digitizing tools and technology Northwestern has access to.
